learning_goal: Draw the boundaries of the mediastinum, split it into its four divisions on the plane of the sternal angle, list the contents of each division in order from front to back, and use that order to say what a mass in a named division is most likely to be and what it will press on first.

structures.name: wall of heart
structures.label: Heart
structures.narration: The middle mediastinum is the heart and its pericardium, and almost nothing else. Define it that way and the other three divisions define themselves: anterior is in front of the pericardium, posterior is behind it, superior is above it. The fibrous pericardium is tough and does not stretch, which is why a small volume of blood in the sac stops the heart while a slow litre of fluid may not.

structures.name: ascending aorta
structures.label: Ascending aorta
structures.narration: Leaves the left ventricle and runs up and to the right, still inside the pericardial sac — which is why a dissection here bleeds into the pericardium and tamponades. Only the coronary arteries come off it.

structures.name: arch of aorta
structures.label: Arch of the aorta
structures.narration: Arches back and to the left, from the sternal angle to the sternal angle — it begins and ends on the same plane. Three branches leave its upper surface in order: brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid, left subclavian. On a chest film its left edge is the aortic knuckle, and a widened one after a road traffic accident means a torn aorta.

structures.name: descending aorta
structures.label: Descending thoracic aorta
structures.narration: Begins on the left side of T4 and works its way to the midline as it descends, giving posterior intercostal arteries on the way. It leaves the thorax behind the diaphragm at T12, through the aortic hiatus — behind, not through, the muscle, which is why its flow is not squeezed by breathing.

structures.name: superior vena cava
structures.label: Superior vena cava
structures.narration: Formed behind the right first costal cartilage by the two brachiocephalic veins, running down on the right of the ascending aorta. It is thin-walled and lies among lymph nodes, so a right upper lobe tumour compresses it: the face and arms swell, the neck veins fill and do not pulsate, and the patient cannot lie flat. The azygos vein joins it just before it enters the atrium.

structures.name: inferior vena cava
structures.label: Inferior vena cava
structures.narration: Pierces the central tendon of the diaphragm at T8 and enters the right atrium after about 2 cm. It has almost no course inside the chest, so it is a middle mediastinal structure and never a posterior one — a favourite trap in a list question.

structures.name: pulmonary artery
structures.label: Pulmonary trunk & arteries
structures.narration: Leaves the right ventricle in front of everything else at the root of the heart and divides under the arch of the aorta. A clot large enough to sit astride that division kills in minutes.

structures.name: esophagus
structures.label: Oesophagus
terms: arch of the aorta indents it
structures.narration: Runs the whole length of the mediastinum in front of the vertebral bodies and behind the trachea, then behind the heart. Three things narrow it in the chest: the arch of the aorta, the left principal bronchus, and the diaphragm at T10. An enlarged left atrium presses on it from in front, which is why a barium swallow was once a cardiology investigation.

structures.label: Oesophageal constriction — arch of the aorta
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: the centre of the CONTACT patch between the oesophagus and the arch of the aorta. One witness, gap 2.02 mm, 50 parent vertices within 6 mm, centroid snapped 0.84 mm; see tools/derive-landmark.mjs --parent FMA7131 --contact FMA3768 --area 6
structures.narration: The first of the three places the oesophagus is narrowed inside the chest. The arch crosses its left side and indents it, and this is the level a swallowed coin or a caustic burn most often stops. It is the highest of the three thoracic constrictions — the measured anchor sits above the bronchial one on the same mesh, which is the geometry agreeing with the textbook order.

structures.label: Oesophageal constriction — left principal bronchus
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: the centre of the CONTACT patch between the oesophagus and the bronchus mesh. One witness, gap 1.16 mm, 51 parent vertices within 6 mm, centroid snapped 2.63 mm; see tools/derive-landmark.mjs --parent FMA7131 --contact FMA7409 --area 6. The catalog holds one generic bronchus mesh, so this is the airway crossing the oesophagus rather than the left principal bronchus specifically — but the patch lies to the left of the midline and below the arch, which is where the left bronchus crosses.
structures.narration: The left principal bronchus crosses in front of the oesophagus and narrows it again, a little below the arch.

structures.label: Oesophageal hiatus (T10)
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: the centre of the CONTACT patch between the oesophagus and the diaphragm — the oesophageal hiatus. One witness, gap 0.31 mm, 325 parent vertices within 6 mm, centroid snapped 6.07 mm; see tools/derive-landmark.mjs --parent FMA7131 --contact FMA13295 --area 6
structures.narration: The last constriction, where the oesophagus passes through the muscle of the right crus at T10 — through the diaphragm, not behind it like the aorta, so this opening does grip. It is the lowest point of the anchor set, which is the geometry confirming the level.

structures.label: Sternal angle — the dividing plane
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: nearest CONTACT point between the manubrium and the body of the sternum — the manubriosternal joint, i.e. the sternal angle (gap 0.11 mm); see tools/derive-mediastinum-landmarks.mjs
structures.narration: The one landmark this whole topic hangs on. The plane through it and the lower border of T4 separates superior from inferior mediastinum. Six things happen on this plane: the trachea divides, the arch of the aorta begins and ends, the azygos vein enters the superior vena cava, the thoracic duct crosses to the left, the pulmonary trunk divides, and the second costal cartilage joins the sternum.

structures.label: Back of the dividing plane (T4/T5)
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: the centre of the CONTACT patch between the fourth thoracic vertebra and the intervertebral disk of the fourth thoracic vertebra — that is, the T4/T5 disc itself, which is what the narration names. One witness, gap 0.07 mm, 260 parent vertices within 8 mm, centroid snapped 2.24 mm; see tools/derive-landmark.mjs --parent FMA9248 --contact FMA13501 --area 8. RE-DERIVED 2026-08-29: the previous definition was the T4-to-descending-aorta contact at a 3.72 mm gap, which the current tool refuses — correctly, because the aorta lies off the front-left of the body and is not the back end of the plane at all.
structures.narration: The back end of the same plane. Draw it from the sternal angle straight back to the disc between T4 and T5, and everything above it is superior mediastinum.

structures.label: Summit of the arch
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: the highest (most superior) vertex of the arch of the aorta, 22.2 mm from the arch's surface centroid; see tools/derive-mediastinum-landmarks.mjs
structures.narration: The top of the arch reaches about the middle of the manubrium — above the sternal angle but below the top of the sternum. That is why the arch is a superior mediastinal structure while the ascending aorta below it is not.

structures.label: Ligamentum arteriosum
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: nearest CONTACT point between the arch of the aorta and the pulmonary artery — where the ligamentum arteriosum runs and the left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks (gap 1.93 mm); see tools/derive-mediastinum-landmarks.mjs
structures.narration: The remnant of the ductus arteriosus, running from the start of the left pulmonary artery to the underside of the arch. The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks around it. That single fact explains why a hoarse voice can be the first sign of a left hilar carcinoma, and why the left nerve is at risk in thoracic surgery while the right one is not.

structures.label: Cavo-atrial junction
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: nearest CONTACT point between the superior vena cava and the wall of the heart — the cavo-atrial junction (gap 0.13 mm); see tools/derive-mediastinum-landmarks.mjs
structures.narration: Where the superior vena cava opens into the right atrium — the point a central line tip should reach and not pass. The sinuatrial node sits in the atrial wall right here, which is why a guidewire pushed too far sets off ectopics.

structures.label: Opening of the inferior vena cava
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: nearest CONTACT point between the inferior vena cava and the wall of the heart — where it enters the right atrium after piercing the diaphragm (gap 0.34 mm); see tools/derive-mediastinum-landmarks.mjs
structures.narration: The inferior vena cava pierces the central tendon of the diaphragm at T8 and enters the right atrium almost at once. Its course inside the chest is only about 2 cm, so it belongs to the middle mediastinum and contributes nothing to the posterior.

structures.label: Aortic hiatus (T12)
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: nearest CONTACT point between the descending aorta and the twelfth thoracic vertebra — the aortic hiatus, where the aorta leaves the posterior mediastinum behind the diaphragm at T12 (gap 0.95 mm); see tools/derive-mediastinum-landmarks.mjs
structures.narration: The lower end of the posterior mediastinum. Three things pass here: the aorta, the thoracic duct and the azygos vein — and because the opening is behind the muscle rather than through it, none of them is squeezed when the diaphragm contracts. Count the openings by their levels: caval at T8, oesophageal at T10, aortic at T12.

structures.name: manubrium
structures.label: Manubrium
structures.narration: The front wall of the superior mediastinum. Its top edge, with the first ribs and T1, is the thoracic inlet — the way in from the neck, which is how a goitre reaches the chest.

structures.name: body of sternum
structures.label: Body of the sternum
structures.narration: The front wall of the inferior mediastinum. The narrow gap between this bone and the pericardium is the whole anterior mediastinum.

structures.name: fourth thoracic vertebra
structures.label: T4 vertebra
structures.narration: The mediastinum is bounded behind by the twelve thoracic vertebral bodies. T4 is the one that matters, because the plane through its lower border divides the space in two.

structures.name: twelfth thoracic vertebra
structures.label: T12 vertebra
structures.narration: The bottom of the posterior mediastinum. Below the diaphragm the same structures continue, but they are abdominal from here.

structures.name: diaphragm
structures.label: Diaphragm
structures.narration: The floor. Three structures leave the mediastinum through or behind it, and the levels count down in even numbers: the inferior vena cava through the central tendon at T8, the oesophagus through the right crus at T10, the aorta behind the muscle at T12. Only the first two are gripped by it.

structures.name: trachea
structures.label: Trachea
structures.narration: Runs down the superior mediastinum and divides on the dividing plane. A trachea pushed off the midline is the physical sign that the whole mediastinum has shifted — away from a tension pneumothorax, towards a collapsed lung.

structures.name: bronchus
structures.label: Principal bronchi
structures.narration: The bifurcation and the roots of the lungs belong to the middle mediastinum, along with the heart. This is where the mediastinal lymph nodes cluster.

structures.name: right brachiocephalic vein
structures.label: Right brachiocephalic vein
structures.narration: The right one is short and almost vertical; the left crosses behind the manubrium to join it, and that crossing is why a sternotomy in a small child is a venous risk. Together they make the superior vena cava.

structures.name: right subclavian artery
structures.label: Right subclavian artery
structures.narration: On the right it comes from the brachiocephalic trunk, and the right recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks around it in the root of the neck — not in the chest. That asymmetry is the reason the two nerves are injured by different diseases.

structures.name: upper lobe of right lung
structures.label: Right upper lobe
structures.narration: The mediastinum is walled on each side by the mediastinal pleura and the lung behind it. Those walls are soft, which is why the mediastinum can be pushed.

structures.name: upper lobe of left lung
structures.label: Left upper lobe
structures.narration: On the left the lung is scooped away in front of the heart, so the pericardium touches the chest wall directly there.

views.title: The space between the lungs
views.narration: The mediastinum is not an organ. It is the space left over in the middle of the chest once the two lungs are taken out: sternum in front, thoracic vertebrae behind, mediastinal pleura on each side, thoracic inlet above, diaphragm below. Everything crossing the chest that is not lung is in here.

views.title: Cut it in two at the sternal angle
views.narration: One plane does all the work. From the sternal angle in front, straight back to the disc between T4 and T5. Above it is the superior mediastinum. Below it is the inferior mediastinum, which the pericardium then divides into three: anterior in front of it, middle which is the pericardium and its contents, posterior behind it. Four divisions from one line you can feel with a finger.

views.title: Superior mediastinum — front to back
views.narration: Learn the superior mediastinum as four layers from front to back. First the thymus. Then the veins: the two brachiocephalic veins joining to make the superior vena cava. Then the arteries: the arch of the aorta with its three branches — brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid, left subclavian. Then the airway and food pipe: trachea in front of oesophagus, with the thoracic duct behind and to the left. Veins in front of arteries, arteries in front of tubes. That order is the answer to most viva questions about this division.

views.title: Middle mediastinum — the heart and what enters it
views.narration: The middle mediastinum is the pericardium and everything in it: the heart, the ascending aorta, the pulmonary trunk, the ends of both venae cavae and the pulmonary veins, the roots of the lungs and the phrenic nerves running down on each side of the pericardium. Note where the two cavae open. The superior comes in from above at the cavo-atrial junction; the inferior pierces the diaphragm at T8 and enters almost immediately, so it barely exists inside the chest at all.

views.title: Anterior mediastinum — a gap, and what fills it
views.narration: Between the body of the sternum and the front of the pericardium there is almost nothing: fat, a few lymph nodes, small vessels, and in a child the lower part of the thymus. It is a thin space, but it is where the classic anterior mediastinal masses sit, and they are remembered as the four Ts — thymoma, teratoma, thyroid that has grown down through the inlet, and terrible lymphoma.

views.title: Posterior mediastinum — behind the heart
views.narration: Behind the pericardium and in front of the vertebral bodies, from the dividing plane down to the diaphragm. Its contents are the descending thoracic aorta, the oesophagus with the vagal trunks on it, the thoracic duct, the azygos and hemiazygos veins, and the sympathetic chains and splanchnic nerves on the sides of the vertebrae. This is why a stab wound in the back that misses the lung can still be fatal, and why an oesophageal tear here floods the space with saliva and gastric contents. Three marks are lit along the oesophagus itself: where the arch of the aorta crosses it, where the left bronchus crosses it lower down, and where it goes through the diaphragm at T10. Those are the three thoracic constrictions, and they are where a swallowed object stops and where a caustic burn is worst. The vagal trunks, the thoracic duct and the azygos veins are named here but are not drawn — no mesh for any of them exists.

views.title: The nerves that explain the symptoms
views.narration: Two nerve rules earn marks and save patients. First: the phrenic nerve runs in front of the root of the lung on the pericardium, the vagus behind it — so a hilar mass takes the vagus first and the diaphragm later. Second: the left recurrent laryngeal nerve leaves the vagus at the arch, hooks under it beside the ligamentum arteriosum, and climbs back up in the groove between trachea and oesophagus. Anything in that window — a carcinoma, a node, an aneurysm, an enlarged left atrium — makes the patient hoarse. The right nerve turns at the subclavian artery in the neck and is spared.

views.title: Reading a shifted mediastinum

ops.kind: compressed by a right upper lobe mass

views.narration: The side walls are soft, so the mediastinum moves. Air trapped under pressure in one pleural cavity pushes it away; a collapsed lung pulls it towards. You read that shift on a film from the trachea and the heart shadow, and at the bedside from the trachea in the suprasternal notch and the apex beat. And because the superior vena cava is the thinnest-walled thing up there, a right upper lobe tumour obstructs it long before it obstructs the aorta beside it.

gaps: There is no pericardium mesh in the catalog, so the middle mediastinum is shown as the heart and the great vessel roots rather than as the sac that actually defines it. This matters more here than in most scenes, because the anterior, middle and posterior divisions are defined by the pericardium: without it, beats 4 to 6 draw their boundaries from the heart's own surface and say so in narration. A pericardium mesh would make this scene substantially better.

CORRECTED 2026-08-29 (audit): this note previously said the oesophagus mesh 'was not available locally', so the oesophagus was carried as an anchor placed by eye on the front of the T4 body — the only unmeasured landmark in the scene, on a scene marked ready. That was false. FMA7131 is in meshes-lite, and the Lungs scene in this same topic was already drawing it. The oesophagus is now a model in the Posterior mediastinum group, and the three thoracic constrictions have been measured off it as contacts: arch of the aorta (gap 2.02 mm), the bronchus mesh (1.16 mm) and the diaphragm (0.31 mm). The measured heights agree with the textbook order — arch above bronchus above hiatus — which is the check on the definitions.

The thymus exists as two lobe meshes and is the front layer of the superior mediastinum and the classic anterior mediastinal mass, but neither lobe was available locally and the scene teaches it in narration only. Adding both lobes would let beat 5 show the four-Ts space with the structure that most often fills it.

No nerve of the thorax is in the catalog: not the phrenic, not the vagus, not the recurrent laryngeals, not the sympathetic chain or the splanchnics. Beat 7 therefore traces the left recurrent laryngeal nerve as a declared concept along the structures it passes, rather than as a model. This is a real teaching loss — the phrenic-in-front, vagus-behind rule is examined constantly and can only be narrated here.

The azygos vein and the thoracic duct are absent from the catalog. Both are named repeatedly, because the azygos arch is one of the six events on the transthoracic plane and the duct is the reason a posterior mediastinal injury causes chylothorax, but neither can be shown.

CORRECTED 2026-08-29 (audit): this note previously said the diaphragm mesh 'was not available locally'. FMA13295 is in meshes-lite and the Lungs scene was already drawing it. The diaphragm is now a context model in Boundaries, so the floor of the mediastinum is drawn rather than implied. What remains true is that the three openings are not separately modelled — the caval opening and the aortic hiatus are taught by their vertebral levels and by the measured contacts of the vessels themselves, and only the oesophageal hiatus has an anchor derived from the diaphragm.
Mediastinal lymph nodes have no meshes anywhere in the catalog, so nodal disease — the commonest reason a student is asked about this space at all — is entirely narrated.

The scene deliberately does not claim to cover the curriculum's 'Great vessels' entry. The arch, the ascending and descending aorta, both cavae and the pulmonary arteries are all present here as the contents that define the divisions, but the branching pattern, the surface markings and the development that a great-vessels scene owes the student are not taught, and marking that entry covered here would hide it.

CORRECTED 2026-08-29 (audit): this note said 'eight of the nine anchors'. There were eight anchors, not nine, and seven of them were measured — the count was written from memory. There are now ten, after the oesophagus was demoted from a guessed anchor to a model and three constrictions were measured off it, and ALL TEN are measured contacts or extremes with the measurement in calibrated_by. All ten remain status 'needs-review' until a human clears them in-app. The ludwig_posterior anchor was the weakest of them — a T4-to-descending-aorta contact at 3.72 mm, which the current derive-landmark.mjs would refuse — and has been re-derived on the T4/T5 intervertebral disc at 0.07 mm, which is the structure the beat-2 narration actually names.
